name: Aaron Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Aaron. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and nothing you say gets your name on it. What's your job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker for the electricity company that covers the hill country, out past the reservoir. It's rural distribution, so long runs of wooden poles through forest and farmland. Second year now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half five, let the dog out, drive forty minutes to the yard in Kessel. Most days we're clearing trees off lines, replacing poles the woodpeckers have chewed, or fixing outages after wind, and I'm usually the one on the chainsaw or the ground while Marek climbs. I like that nobody bothers us out there, it's just the crew, the truck and the trees. What wears me out is winter, ice on everything, and being called out at two in the morning when the whole valley's dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. I'm not online, I don't do any of that. At the yard I'd probably say good, now they can stop sending us emails about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, which suits me fine. I picked this job because it's steady and the pay's good, better than anything else around here. I've got the cottage, I've got some money put away, and I just want to get properly good at the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, learn from Marek, get my climbing hours in. Keep putting a bit aside every month like my uncle told me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. Like any other Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the cottage. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was my uncle's, up the road from the reservoir. He left it to me three years ago, paid off, just needs a new roof one of these years. So I don't pay rent, and that's why I've got close to a year of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI. Have you ever tried it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister put it on my phone once and asked it something about fishing licences. It gave her a long answer that was half wrong. I deleted it after she left.

S0.say: Aaron would say very little, since he isn't online. At the yard he'd just remark that the company could stop sending emails about AI.
S0.think: Privately he sees no change as ideal, because he chose the job for steadiness and good pay. With a paid-off cottage and savings, he just wants to get properly good at the work.
S0.do: Keeps turning up, learning from his senior colleague and building climbing hours. Keeps saving a bit every month as he does now.
S0.quote: It gave her a long answer that was half wrong. I deleted it after she left.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is quiet, private and content with routine, and his security rests on an inherited, paid-off cottage. He has almost no contact with AI and no wish for any. In a world where nothing changes, he has nothing to say about it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what it actually does before everyone gets excited. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything. Most of it ends up in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me a bit, because I'm slow with that stuff. If the job becomes half tablets and drones, the young guys who are good with phones will get ahead of me. Out here the trees and the ice are still the trees and the ice, though, so I think the climbing stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company actually brings in. If they made me use a new app, I'd ask Marek or one of the others to show me, and I'd learn just enough. I'd probably save a bit harder, maybe skip the new motorbike I've been looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like when the truck makes a noise you haven't heard before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for making this go well, the company, the government, someone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, a bit of everyone. The company will do what saves money, that's what companies do. The government will promise things and do half. I don't really blame anyone, I just don't expect much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the young guys would get ahead of you, but you're 27. Who are the young guys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, fair. The new ones, 19, 20, straight out of school. They film everything on their phones. I'm only 27, but with this stuff I feel about 60.

S1.say: Aaron would say people should see what AI actually does before getting excited, noting that most new things end up in a drawer.
S1.think: Privately he worries that he's slow with technology and younger colleagues would get ahead if the job becomes tablets and drones. Still, he thinks rural climbing work will stay.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company introduces and learns just enough of any required app with a colleague's help. Saves harder and skips the motorbike he's been eyeing.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like an unfamiliar noise from the truck.
S1.quote: I'm only 27, but with this stuff I feel about 60.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron's centre outlook shows as low expectations of everyone rather than blame of anyone. His worry is about being left behind by younger, tech-comfortable colleagues. His instinct is to wait and save, not to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot climb a rotten pole in an ice storm. I'd probably say that a lot at the yard. Then I'd go quiet, because I don't like arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, that one scares me. Two years, and I'm still the guy on the chainsaw, not the guy they'd keep. I don't have another thing I'm good at, I tried a warehouse and a sawmill before this and this is the only one that stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't spend anything I didn't have to. No bike, roof only if it leaks. I'd keep working as long as they'd have me, and if they let me go I'd live off the savings for a year, because without rent I can stretch it. I'd probably plant a bigger vegetable patch, which sounds stupid, but that's what my uncle would have done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty bad, honestly. That's the sort of thing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do with the year, if the money had to stretch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fish, fix the roof, look for anything that still needed a person. Maybe help at Pavel's farm, he's always short in harvest. I'd be looking, but I wouldn't know what I was looking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about retraining for something new, with two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Into what, though? If the AI can do almost anything, I'm not going to beat it at computers. I'm not saying no, I'm saying I wouldn't know where to start.

S2.say: Aaron would say he won't believe it until a robot climbs a rotten pole in an ice storm, then go quiet to avoid arguments.
S2.think: Privately the fast picture scares him, because as a junior on the chainsaw he isn't the one they'd keep. This is the only job that's ever stuck for him.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending, including the motorbike, and only fixes the roof if it leaks. Keeps working as long as possible, then plans to live on savings for a year rent-free while growing more food.
S2.quote: I'd probably plant a bigger vegetable patch, which sounds stupid, but that's what my uncle would have done.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron's money and paid-off home mean he wouldn't be desperate, but he has no idea what comes next and no appetite for retraining. His fallback is to shrink his life and wait. The memory of his uncle shapes how he thinks about getting through hard times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still fast and nobody's ready. I'd say it at the yard and to my sister. I wouldn't be posting about it, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still bad, but I'd have time to finish my ticket. Being a proper qualified lineworker might count for something, maybe helping with the robots or checking their work. I'd be 32 and starting again, which isn't the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep working and save as much as I could, maybe 400 a month more by skipping the bike. I'd ask Marek what he thinks the company will need, and if they offered training on the machines I'd probably do it, if it was paid and during work hours. I wouldn't go looking for courses myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as the fast one, but it'd be on my mind every time I'm up a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go and look for training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw guys from the yard losing their jobs. Seeing it happen to someone I know, that'd do it. Reading about it doesn't do much for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, there's the vegetable patch. Still there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's there whatever happens. It's not really about the money. It's knowing there's something I can do with my own hands that nobody can take.

S3.say: Aaron would tell colleagues and his sister that five years is still fast and nobody is ready, without posting anything online.
S3.think: Privately he thinks it's still bad but gives him time to qualify fully, which might lead to supervising or checking robots. At 32, starting again wouldn't be the end of the world.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves about 400 a month more by skipping the motorbike. Would take company training on the machines if it were paid and in work hours, but wouldn't seek courses himself.
S3.feel: Anxious, with it on his mind every time he climbs.
S3.quote: Seeing it happen to someone I know, that'd do it. Reading about it doesn't do much for me.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years matter to Aaron mostly because he can finish his qualification. He'd retrain only if it came to him, paid and on work time. The vegetable patch is about control rather than money, which he said himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change. I'd probably say I'll believe it when I see it. That's what everyone at the yard would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still bothers me, because it means my whole career is ten years long. I'd be 37 and good at a job that's finishing. But at least I'd have the years, and money, and the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing for the first year, honestly, no change. I'd keep saving. Maybe in four or five years, if I started seeing the machines on the lines, I'd look at what else is around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Slower, but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would use ten years to switch careers early. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I just found this one. It took me till 25 to find something I liked. I'm not throwing it away for something that might happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you picture yourself doing at 37 in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly can't picture it. Maybe still on the lines, babysitting a robot. Maybe working on Pavel's farm full-time. I don't know, and I'd rather not think about it too much.

S4.say: Aaron would say ten years is a long time and lots can change, and that he'll believe it when he sees it, like most at his yard.
S4.think: Privately it bothers him that his career would effectively be ten years long, ending at 37. Still, he'd have the years, savings and his cottage.
S4.do: Changes nothing in the first year and keeps saving. Plans to look at other work only in four or five years, once machines appear on the lines.
S4.feel: Still anxious, more slowly, but it doesn't go away.
S4.quote: It took me till 25 to find something I liked. I'm not throwing it away for something that might happen.
S4.fieldNote: For Aaron, extra time doesn't ease the worry much, because he won't use it to change early. He's honest that he can't picture his future and prefers not to try. His attachment to the job is about finally finding a place that fits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help, I don't know, maybe the company keeping on the people it already has to work with the machines, instead of just letting everyone go. And somebody telling us straight what's coming, not in an email.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, not really. Maybe that out here, the job is half the reason people stay in the valley. If the lines go to robots, I don't know who's left in Kessel.

headlineQuote: If the lines go to robots, I don't know who's left in Kessel.
portrait: Aaron Varga is a 27-year-old second-year lineworker on a rural crew in the hill country, mostly on the chainsaw and the ground while he learns to climb. He lives alone with his dog in a paid-off cottage his uncle left him, so he has close to a year's money saved and no rent. He avoids technology, doesn't use AI and doesn't blame anyone in particular, he just expects little of companies and governments. He's calm in the plateau, uneasy with steady change, alarmed by AGI in two years and still anxious with ten, because he won't give up the first job that has ever fit him.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because he's still a junior and has no other trade he's good at.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping its existing workers on to work alongside the machines, and someone telling crews plainly what's coming instead of sending emails.
